survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PIAAC PSTRE process data from the second cluster (PS2) administered to adults in five countries (GBR, IRL, JPN, NLD, USA). The analytic sample is restricted to respondents assigned to PS2 and further excludes cases with at least one nonresponse (NR) sequence pattern in the LCS analysis, yielding a final LCS sample of 5302. The manuscript does not report whether PIAAC sampling/survey weights or replicate weights were applied in the computation of indicators (SM, SSD, EM, ESD) or in the ANOVA/correlation analyses, so weight usage cannot be confirmed. Because the analysis is based on derived process indicators and classical association tests rather than PV-based achievement modeling, analysts should consult the PIAAC technical documentation for appropriate weight variables (e.g., student/sampling weights) if population-representative inference is required.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables in this study are process-derived behavioral indicators (similarity/efficiency and their consistency) and PSTRE proficiency levels/scores, rather than PV-based cognitive achievement outcomes with an explicit PV framework. Missingness is handled by excluding respondents with at least one nonresponse (NR) sequence pattern from the LCS analysis, but the paper does not describe a general missing-data strategy for other variables (e.g., background covariates) beyond this sequence-based exclusion. Therefore, missing-data handling is treated as a reporting gap for any additional missingness not tied to the NR sequence criterion.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study uses PIAAC PSTRE PS2 process and response data from seven interactive PSTRE items administered in five countries (GBR, IRL, JPN, NLD, USA). The initial respondent sample for the current study is 7462 adults assigned to PS2. Respondents are excluded from the LCS analysis if they have at least one occurrence of a shortest observed action sequence pattern interpreted as nonresponse (NR), which removes 2160 respondents and yields a final LCS analytic sample of 5302. Additionally, keyboard-related actions are collapsed into a generalized keystroke label ('key') to address cross-language input differences, and all seven PSTRE items are presented in the same order with no imposed time/action limits.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC PS2 PSTRE (adult problem solving in technology-rich environments), 2012-2017, 7 interactive items (process data)
main_findings.target_variable: Problem-solving proficiency (PSTRE score/level) predicted by behavioral patterns
top_predictors: Behavioral pattern: similarity to optimal action sequences (SM) and consistency of similarity (SSD)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Correlation between PSTRE proficiency scores and similarity indicator: r=0.79 (positive). Similarity increases across proficiency levels: average similarity rises from 0.39 to 0.83 from below level 1 to level 3. Efficiency-proficiency relationship: no strong relationship reported; within proficiency level 3, consistency of efficiency band is narrowest (ESD=0.21). Additional analysis (Behavioral pattern: similarity to optimal action sequences (SM) and consistency of similarity (SSD)): Country differences in similarity: one-way ANOVA F(4, 5297)=39.52, P<0.001; consistency of similarity: ANOVA F(4, 5297)=9.10, P<0.001 (Japan lower than other countries). Gender differences in similarity-group membership: women more likely in low/moderate similarity by ~4 and ~3 percentage points; men more likely in high similarity by ~7 percentage points. Age differences in similarity-group membership: ANOVA F(2, 5299)=69.53, P<0.001 (younger higher similarity).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC PS2 PSTRE process data, the study leveraged behavioral similarity (SM) and its consistency (SSD) alongside demographic and ICT familiarity to relate action-sequence strategies to PSTRE proficiency, finding a strong positive association between PSTRE scores and similarity (r=0.79) and a clear increasing trend in similarity from low to high proficiency levels. This indicates that training adults to follow more optimal, information-seeking interaction strategies in digital tasks may improve PSTRE-relevant problem-solving performance, though the study is correlational and does not establish causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: This Computers & Education study uses PIAAC PSTRE process data from the second cluster (PS2) administered to adults in five countries (England/Northern Ireland, Ireland, Japan, the Netherlands, and the United States) on seven interactive PSTRE items. The authors derive four cross-item behavioral indicators from log-file action sequences using longest common subsequence (LCS) alignment to ex-ante optimal reference sequences: similarity (SM), consistency of similarity (SSD), efficiency (EM), and consistency of efficiency (ESD). They exclude respondents with at least one nonresponse (NR) shortest-sequence pattern from the LCS analysis, reducing the analytic sample from 7462 to 5302. Results show significant country differences in similarity (ANOVA F(4,5297)=39.52, P<0.001) and a strong positive correlation between PSTRE proficiency scores and similarity (r=0.79), while efficiency shows a weaker relationship. The paper does not report a general missing-data strategy beyond the NR exclusion and does not describe survey-weight usage, limiting population-representative inference.
